title: The Effectiveness of Socratic Dialogue in Developing Oral Communication Skills Among Malaysian AFL Learners: An Applied Linguistic Study
abstract: This study explored the effectiveness of Socratic dialogue as a pedagogical approach in enhancing the oral communication skills of Malaysian AFL university learners in the context of AFL instruction. The study employed a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control group design with a 13-week treatment period that involved 124 Malaysian AFL university students randomly selected at the class level between 2 groups: Socratic dialogue intervention group and conventional oral communication instruction control group. Oral communication skills were evaluated based on four criteria: fluent speech and delivery, critical elaboration of discourse, interactional pragmatic competence and argumentative coherence. The results of analysis of covariance showed statistically significant gains for Socratic dialogue participants on all four skill dimensions, with the highest gains in the critical discourse elaboration dimension and the argumentative coherence dimension. title: Reflective Practices and Learner Engagement in L2 Writing: Perceptions and Associations Among Saudi EFL Learners
abstract: Reflective practices and learner engagement have received increasing attention in L2 writing research due to their importance in promoting self-regulated learning and writing development. This study investigated Saudi female EFL learners’ perceptions of reflective practices and learner engagement in L2 writing, along with the correlation between these two constructs. The study employed a quantitative cross-sectional survey using a questionnaire administered to 545 Saudi female EFL university students. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson’s correlation coefficient, and one-way ANOVA. The results revealed generally positive perceptions of reflective practices and relatively high levels of learner engagement in L2 writing. Cognitive engagement received the highest ratings, whereas behavioral engagement showed comparatively lower levels. Furthermore, a statistically significant positive relationship was identified between reflective practices and learner engagement. The findings suggest that reflective activities may support learners’ engagement, self-monitoring, and writing development in L2 writing contexts. title: A Lexico-Semantic Analysis of Persian Loanwords in Shajara-i Terakime
abstract: The linguistic study of Turkic written heritage, historical manuscripts and epic texts is essential for understanding the development and evolution of the language. This article examines Shajara-i Terakime written by Abu’l-Gazi Bahadur Khan in the 17th century, a medieval monument that provides valuable data on the history, culture, ethnography and toponymy of Turkic peoples. The text represents an Oguz-nama version written in Arabic script. Alongside Old Turkic vocabulary, the lexical structure of the chronicle contains a significant number of Arabic, Persian and Mongolian elements. This article analyses the lexico-semantic features of Persian loanwords found in the work and identifies their usage in Modern Kazakh, as well as in Kazakh folklore and the poetry of zhyrau. While Arab-Persian borrowings are often treated as a single group in historical lexicology, here Persian elements are examined separately as an independent lexical layer. title: Resistance and Identity Negotiation: Strategies of LGBT Resistance to Heteronormative Power in Selected Indonesian Novels
abstract: This research aims to reveal strategies of resistance in the form of resistance and negotiation against practices of power directed at LGBT figures in Indonesian novels, and to show the role of the novel as a space for articulating LGBT resistance within the configuration of Indonesian socio‑political power. The study employs a descriptive textual qualitative design with a literary sociology and gender studies approach, using Michel Foucault’s concept of power relations as the main theoretical framework. The corpus consists of six post-Reform era Indonesian novels selected for the prominence of LGBT themes and conflicts related to stigmatization, violence, and the regulation of sexuality. Research data comprises textual excerpts that depict power relations, stigmatization, exclusion, and various forms of resistance and negotiation carried out by LGBT figures. Data was collected through heuristic reading and the read-and-record method, then organized into data tables, and finally analyzed through in-depth reading and hermeneutic interpretation. title: Beyond Directivity: Directives as Strategies of Domination in Henrik Ibsen's Hedda Gabler
abstract: This study investigates directives as linguistic strategies of domination in Henrik Ibsen's (1890) Hedda Gabler. The paper draws on two analytical approaches: first, speech act theory, specifically Searle's (1976) categorization of directive speech acts, to demonstrate how directives are pragmatically augmented to communicate specific purposes within interpersonal power relations rather than their ordinary perceived functions of commanding, requesting, and questioning; and second, the rapport management framework (Spencer-Oatey, 2002, 2005), which provides a basis for investigating how directive choices influence interpersonal relations and domination. The paper adopts a qualitative pragmatic approach to analyze selected conversational turns from the play and to show how directives are employed to negotiate unequal power relations and thus to exercise domination. The analytical focus is on four types of directives: imperatives, interrogatives, modal directives, and indirect/polite directives, to examine how these types of directives acquire manipulative force through contextual factors, including power relations and communicative intentions. title: Semiotics and Discourse Analysis in A German Woman in the State of Terror: Extremism, Family, and Digital Space
abstract: The present study examines the audiovisual text of the documentary A German Woman in the State of Terror, exploring its utilisation of language, image and discourse to re-represent extremism. The film's technique is predicated on the assumption that the narrative of a German teenage girl who joins ISIS is not merely presented as a matter of security, but as a complex crisis involving familial, identity-related, and digital dimensions, as well as a complex discourse. The present study employs a descriptive-analytical approach, drawing upon the concepts of linguistic semiotics, visual semiotics and discourse analysis. The analysis focuses on specific key shots that function as dense signifying units. Evidence from a single site indicates that the film organises its meaning through its use of significant binaries, such as family/organization, home/war, digital presence/bodily absence, and alleged state/actual devastation. title: Who Regulates AI Better? Exploring AI Self-Regulated Learning Among Novice and Experienced Vietnamese EFL Teachers
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly transformed teacher professional learning in English as a foreign language (EFL) education. However, relatively limited research has examined how teachers strategically regulate and sustain their AI-related learning processes, particularly across different stages of professional experience. This study investigated AI self-regulated learning (AI-SRL) among novice and experienced Vietnamese in-service EFL teachers. An explanatory sequential mixed methods design was employed. Quantitative data were collected from 1,108 Vietnamese in-service EFL teachers using the AI-SRL Scale, followed by semi-structured interviews with 10 teachers. The quantitative findings revealed that novice teachers demonstrated significantly higher levels of AI-SRL than experienced teachers, particularly in task planning, self-monitoring, and self-evaluation. Notably, no statistically significant differences were identified in help seeking and institutional support. title: The Linguistic Personality of Bauyrzhan Momyshuly in Ä. Nūrshaıyqov’s Truth and Legend
abstract: This article analyzes the linguistic personality of Bauyrzhan Momyshuly in Äzılhan Nūrshaıyqov’s novel Aqiqat pen añyz (Truth and Legend) from the perspectives of anthropocentric and cognitive linguistics. The aim of the study is to identify the lexical, discursive, and national-cultural features of the character’s speech, as well as to describe his worldview and communicative identity through linguistic data. The research material included the character’s direct speech, dialogic structures, military terminology, emotional-expressive vocabulary, metaphorical expressions, and code-switching found in the novel. The study employed textual analysis, discourse analysis, cognitive analysis, and pragmalinguistic methods. The results of the research demonstrated that military vocabulary in Bauyrzhan Momyshuly’s speech carries not only professional meaning but also ideological and moral significance. Directive structures reveal the character’s leadership qualities and discipline-based communicative model, while emotional-expressive vocabulary reflects his spiritual nature and moral values. title: Linguistic Landscape of Mosque Names in Yogyakarta City: Language Policy and Ideological Construction
abstract: Language in public spaces reflects community identity, culture, and ideology. It can be seen in mosque naming that shows linguistic and value diversity. Using qualitative approach with a descriptive method, this study aims to analyze linguistic patterns in mosque naming in Yogyakarta City and to reveal their relationship with language policy and ideological construction in public space. The research data consist of mosque names in Yogyakarta City, Indonesia, which were collected by recording mosque names and documenting mosque signboards as visual data. The data were then analyzed through several systematic stages. The findings show that linguistic patterns in mosque naming in Yogyakarta City are dominated by Arabic in monolingual forms, followed by Javanese and Indonesian, as well as a small number of bilingual and trilingual patterns. The dominance of Arabic indicates the strong influence of religious values in public space. Meanwhile, the use of Javanese reflects the continuity of local cultural identity, and Indonesian represents national identity. title: Modeling Novice Academic Discourse Across Disciplines: A Five-Dimensional Linguistic Framework for Tracing Disciplinary Voice in Law and Education
abstract: This study examines how novice L2 writers construct disciplinary voice across epistemologically divergent domains—Law and English Education—using the Five-Dimensional Disciplinary Discourse Model (5D-DDM). Drawing on two purpose-built corpora (75 texts each), a corpus-assisted analysis traced rhetorical variation across five dimensions. In Education, students exhibited (1) a relational stance through collective self-mention and cautious modality; (2) agentive positioning with participatory reader engagement; (3) hybrid patterning via SVO syntax, classificatory noun phrases, and evaluative collocations; (4) restrained affect with moderate appreciation and minimal judgment; and (5) expansive interdiscursivity through media-cultural recontextualization. Conversely, Law texts displayed (1) a categorical stance marked by suppressed self-mention and booster-driven certainty; (2) depersonalized authorship with monologic reader positioning; (3) fixed legal collocations, procedural passives, and normative modality; (4) codified judgment with affective suppression and limited appreciation; and (5) compressed interdiscursivity anchored in statutory authority. title: Reclaiming Voice: English Language Teachers, Arabic Publishing, and Academic Legitimacy in Kuwait
abstract: This study examines how English-dominant publication expectations shape English language teachers’ professional voice, linguistic agency, and perceptions of research purpose in Kuwait. Drawing on an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, the study combines questionnaire responses from 50 MA- and PhD-qualified English language instructors with semi-structured interviews with 10 participants. The analysis is informed by critical applied linguistics, language policy, linguistic capital, language ideology, and epistemic justice. Findings show that teachers do not reject English as a language of international academic visibility, but they question its dominance as the sole recognized medium for promotion and scholarly legitimacy. While participants acknowledged the professional value of English-medium publication, many also viewed Arabic-medium and bilingual publication as essential for improving local accessibility, policy relevance, and educational impact. title: Diglossic Influence on Standard Arabic Production: Word Order and Verb Agreement in Narratives by Saudi Najdi Preschool Children
abstract: This study examines the influence of diglossia on the production of Standard Arabic (SA) by 29 Saudi Najdi preschool children aged 4 to 6 years old. It explores their ability to produce sentences in SA, identifies whether subject–verb–object (SVO) or verb–subject–object (VSO) word order is more prevalent, and examines patterns of verb agreement. Data were gathered by asking participants to retell three stories presented in SA. Both quantitative and qualitative analyses were used in the morphosyntactic analysis. The findings show that despite preschool children’s limited, informal exposure to SA through television and other media, they were able to produce sentences in this variety. VSO word order was more frequently produced than SVO, but no word order was statistically dominant in the data. The descriptive data showed slightly higher rates of VSO than SVO word order in SA sentences and in utterances with diglossic intra-sentential code-switching, whereas SVO word order was more frequent in sentences combining SA and shared forms.
